name: The Cull Road
platesLines: With a clank, both plates sink into the bank.
Chains draw taut out of the river. The old ferry-bridge comes up, streaming, and settles across the water.
firstVisit: The road north narrows to a lane between the pines.
It has been worn very smooth, by a great many small feet.

T: Pines, close on both sides of the road. Nowhere to run to.
<: The road back to Warrior City.
c: A lantern on a post, a candle burning in it.
Somebody keeps it lit. Every night, for whoever's walking.
1: A milestone: TWO MILES FROM THE CITY.
Carved underneath, small: I CAN STILL SEE THE WALLS.
2: A milestone: THREE MILES FROM THE CITY.
Carved underneath, smaller: CAN'T SEE THE WALLS NOW. GOOD.
4: A child's shoe, in the long grass. Just the one.
x: The tithe-takers' fire, still warm. They never stay long.
They don't like this road either. Nobody does.
|: The deserters' palisade: sharpened stakes, all along the bank.
Built to keep the tithe-takers out. It mostly did.
7: What's left of the gate, hanging off one hinge. Smashed in from this side.
Whatever did it didn't use hands.
Y: A wooden sword, snapped in two. Somebody practised with it very hard.
Not hard enough, the tithe-takers said.
;: Reeds, as tall as a twelve-year-old.
~: The river, fast and brown. The old bridge went downstream years ago.
Nobody has built a new one. That was also the idea.
=: The old ferry-bridge, sunk on its chains just under the water.
Two chains run up out of the river to two plates in the bank. It only rises from this side.
P: An iron plate in the mud, chained to the ferry-bridge. It wants something heavy on it.
Something heavier than a child. That was the whole idea.
O: A boulder. Heavy. You could push it, if you leaned in.

lines: BY ORDER OF THE KING. THE TITHE OF CHILDREN, AT TWELVE:
STRONG: TO THE YARD. FED, HOUSED, TRAINED. FAMILY MOVED TO THE CITY.
NOT STRONG: TO THE CAMP. NO RATIONS. NO COIN. NO COMING BACK.
RUNAWAYS TO BE WALKED BACK DOWN. AGAIN.
Scratched underneath, at about elbow height: "I'll come back strong."
A mile-post: ONE MILE FROM THE CITY.
Carved under it, small and careful: I WAS 12. I WAS NOT STRONG ENOUGH.
Under that, in a different hand: ME NEITHER.
And under that: ME NEITHER. And under that, and under that, all the way down into the grass.
A plank nailed to a pine, notched all the way up. Heights, with names.
ODO, 12. BRIDGET, 12. HAL, 12 AND A HALF.
The Yard's mark is nailed near the top, in iron. Nobody's notch comes close to it.

objects.name: Ada
lines: I come up here every year. On the day.
I count them going past, and I wave. You're meant to wave. Somebody has to.

answer: My girl. She went down this road eleven years ago. Twelve, and small for it.
She'll be twenty-three now. Taller, I should think. I'd like to see that.
So they can see the way back up.
Nobody's used it yet. You don't put a lantern out just because nobody's used it.

questions.ask: What's it like at the camp?
answer: Not much food. Not much warmth. No money at all. No fighting, though.
I tell myself the last part is the important part. Most days it works.

questions.ask: She wasn't strong enough. That's on her.
answer: No. It's on whoever decided strong was the only thing worth being.
* She turns back to the road, and waves at nobody.

lines: The tithe-takers didn't come this year. They say the king's gone.
I'm walking down to the camp. Then the two of us are walking back up. Slowly. She's taller than me now.

objects.name: Lark
lines: Shh. Shadows at the gate. They came up out of the river mist a month back, and nobody's asked them to leave.
I'm the camp's scout. I scout. Mostly from in here.

answer: The ferry-bridge. It's sunk on its chains. Weigh down both plates in the bank and up it comes.
The tithe-takers roll those boulders on, cross over, and roll them off again behind them.
It only rises from this side. They thought that was very clever.

questions.ask: How did you end up at the camp?
answer: Walked down this road at twelve. Too short, the yardmaster said. Bad eyes.
I can see a shadow at forty paces in the dark. I'm just short. That's not an eye thing.
The tithe-takers still walk the road, looking for runaways.
Runaways from where, I ask you. We're already away. That's the whole complaint.

questions.ask: A scout who hides in the reeds? Coward.
answer: Brave scouts get seen. Seen scouts get walked back down.
* He sinks a little lower into the reeds, on principle.

lines: You raised it! Last time that took two tithe-takers and a mule.
Go on over. Mind the roses at the camp. Old Morrow has opinions about feet.
